item.title: Applying Trauma-Informed Care in Psychedelic Therapy
item.description:
Trauma

Applying Trauma-Informed Care in Psychedelic Therapy

How to achieve safety across the psychedelic care experience.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Trauma-informed care (TIC) recognizes the ongoing effects of traumatic experiences.
  • Trauma-informed psychedelic care is an approach that shapes the entire therapeutic process.
  • TIC should be applied at all phases of psychedelic study: preparation, dosing, and integration.
  • All patient-facing staff must have an understanding of trauma to flexibly tailor the patient experience.

By Sara So, L.C.P.C.

Psychedelic experiences can be intense and unpredictable, leaving patients especially vulnerable. For people with a history of trauma, that vulnerability requires thoughtful care. That’s where trauma-informed care (TIC) comes in.

Trauma-informed care recognizes that traumatic experiences can have lasting effects on a person’s emotions, relationships, body, and sense of safety. It encourages providers to create conditions that promote safety, choice, trust, and a sense of control while reducing the risk of re-traumatization.

These principles are particularly important in psychedelic-assisted therapy.

What Is Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy?

Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) combines a psychedelic substance with psychological support or psychotherapy. Depending on the treatment or research protocol, therapeutic approaches may include Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), or other forms of psychotherapy.

PAT generally includes three stages:

  1. Preparation. The patient and therapist build a therapeutic relationship, discuss what to expect, establish boundaries, and prepare for the emotional and physical effects of the psychedelic.

  2. Dosing. The same therapist supports the patient during the psychedelic experience, helping maintain physical and psychological safety while encouraging an inner-directed experience.

  3. Integration. Afterward, the patient and therapist process the experience, make sense of what emerged, and consider how insights from the session might be incorporated into everyday life.

The patient’s mindset, often called “set," and the physical and interpersonal environment, known as “setting," are important throughout psychedelic treatment.

In the United States, most psychedelics remain Schedule I controlled substances at the federal level, with ketamine being a notable exception. As a result, much PAT involving substances such as psilocybin and MDMA occurs within clinical research or other legally authorized settings. Clinical trials are standardized and time-limited, which can create additional challenges when tailoring care to an individual patient’s needs.

How Trauma Can Surface During Psychedelic Therapy

Trauma can result from a single overwhelming event or from repeated experiences over time. Complex trauma generally involves repeated or prolonged traumatic experiences, often within important relationships or involving caregivers or authority figures.

Trauma can emerge during any stage of psychedelic therapy, just as it can during traditional psychotherapy. Psychedelics add another layer because they can intensify emotions, memories, bodily sensations, and perceptions while changing a person’s usual sense of control.

A patient may experience fear, disorientation, helplessness, or difficult memories with unusual intensity. Trauma-informed care helps therapists prepare for these possibilities rather than simply react when distress occurs.

What Does Trauma-Informed Psychedelic Care Look Like?

Trauma-informed psychedelic care is an approach that shapes the entire therapeutic process. At its core, it means protecting patient agency, maintaining relational safety, respecting boundaries, and treating consent as an ongoing process.

Before a dosing session, for example, the therapist and patient might discuss grounding techniques that feel helpful, as well as words, behaviors, or interactions that could increase distress. Such conversations allow the patient to have a meaningful voice in their care before entering an altered state.

Preparation: Building Safety and Trust

Preparation can be particularly important for people with complex trauma because previous experiences may affect trust, relationships, and feelings of safety.

Trauma-informed preparation can include additional preparatory sessions, practicing grounding techniques, discussing how trauma can show up emotionally and physically, and creating a plan for managing distress during the dosing experience. When significant safety concerns arise, dosing may need to be delayed or canceled.

Planning for Supportive Touch

Patients may be unusually vulnerable during a psychedelic experience.

If supportive touch might be used as a grounding technique, the patient and therapist should discuss it beforehand. Examples could include hand-holding or placing a hand on the patient’s wrist, arm, shoulder, or upper back.

Consent should be specific and ongoing.

Alternatives can also be planned. A patient who does not want direct touch might prefer to hold one end of a cushion while the therapist holds the other, providing a sense of connection without physical contact.

Planning the possibilities in advance gives patients greater agency during a time when communicating their needs may become difficult.

Dosing: Maintaining Consent and Safety

During dosing, the therapist continues nurturing the relationship and safety planning established during preparation.

Because psychedelics can produce disorientation, vulnerability, or a reduced ability to make decisions, therapists need to remain attentive to both verbal communication and nonverbal cues.

For example, if supportive touch is being used and a patient suddenly tenses, becomes still, changes their breathing, pulls away, or stops speaking, the therapist should recognize that something may have changed. Previously given consent should not be treated as permanent permission. The therapist can stop, physically create space, and verbally explain what they are doing.

Clear boundaries, well-defined roles, ongoing consent, and careful attention to the patient’s responses help protect both physical and emotional safety.

Integration: Supporting What Happens Afterward

Trauma-informed care doesn’t end after the dosing session. Difficult emotions or trauma-related symptoms may emerge hours or days later.

During integration, the therapist helps the patient understand and respond to what surfaced during the experience. Support may include previously identified coping strategies such as breathing exercises, grounding practices, familiar routines, and trusted social support. If significant trauma-related symptoms emerge, additional integration sessions or specialized trauma-informed mental health treatment may be appropriate.

Ideally, these resources are identified during preparation so patients already know where they can turn if they need additional support.

Possible trauma responses during psychedelic therapy
Source: Sunstone Therapies

A Framework for Safer Psychedelic Care

Trauma-informed care is more than a strategy for managing a difficult psychedelic experience. It is a framework for designing care throughout the process.

It asks therapists and care teams to consider safety, trust, consent, choice, boundaries, power, and individual needs at every stage, from preparation through dosing, integration, and aftercare.

Because psychedelic experiences can place people in unusually vulnerable states, understanding how trauma may interact with those experiences is essential. Incorporating trauma-informed principles throughout psychedelic-assisted therapy can create a safer therapeutic environment while helping patients maintain a sense of agency in their own care.

Sara So, L.C.P.C., is a psychotherapist with more than a decade of experience in academic research. They hold a Master of Health Science from Johns Hopkins University, a Master of Science from Loyola University Maryland, and a Bachelor of Arts from Pennsylvania State University. Prior to joining Sunstone Therapies, they served as a Psychiatric Therapist at the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research at Johns Hopkins University.

item.title: Supporting the Non-Genetically Related Parent
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Supporting the Non-Genetically Related Parent

Non-genetically linked parents can easily feel ignored, even by themselves.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Communication, mutal decision making, and building traditions can help families who use donor conception.
  • Bonding is not dependent on genetics.
  • Feelings about being genetically connected or not often go unspoken in donor conception families.
Source: Freepik/Magnific

When couples use donor conception to build their family, they often do not share the same experience. These differences are often more pronounced when one partner cannot conceive using their eggs or sperm, but even when that is not the case, as in a same sex couple, the non-genetically related parent may be overlooked, or their feelings may be minimized by their partner or by themselves. This can result in difficulties for the individual and for the relationship.

In my three decades of practice, I have occasionally seen couples where the genetically linked parent is more distressed about the need for donor eggs or sperm than the non-genetically linked parent, however, this is not common. More often, the non-genetically linked parent absorbs the stress of treatment, the uncertainty of the process, and fears about using the genetics of someone they don’t know to create their family. They may have feelings of loss about not being able to use their genetics, worry that the child may not bond with them, and feel concerned that the child, or outside world, will view the genetically linked parent as the “real” parent.

These experiences may be shared within the couple, or the non-genetically linked parent may carry their fears quietly. They may wonder what it will feel like at Thanksgiving when relatives stare at the child looking for a family resemblance, or how they will respond to strangers asking probing questions. They may also wonder how they will be a good parent with all of these issues and fears.

While these experiences are not uncommon, they often live in the background and are not always shared. This can create tension for the parent and between the couple.

The truth is that bonding does not happen just because we share genetics. Connection grows in the thousands of small moments between a parent and child over time. Although the non-genetically related parent may worry about bonding, it is important to hold on to the understanding that the child will see them as their parent. Through their relationship, they will live through the ups and downs of family life. Will there be moments of sadness, insecurity, or jealously? Possibly. But those feelings will ease over time as the non-genetically related parent becomes more comfortable with the family they have helped to create, and their place in it.

Given this reality, if you are the non-genetically related parent, staying connected to your partner and taking care of yourself are essential. Here are five things that may help:

1. Name your fears

Vague anxiety is often more difficult to sort out than naming a specific fear. Try to identify what you feel afraid of. Perhaps you are worried about feeling that your family will be disconnected from your long line of Irish relatives, that your in laws won’t see the child as yours, or that your child will not share your musical talent. These feelings are natural. Sharing them with your partner can help you feel less alone with them and reduce the likelihood of your upset surfacing in unhelpful ways.

2. Talk to your partner

As these feelings persist, jealousy or resentment can build. A conversation discussing traits your partner shares with your child at a cocktail party can turn an otherwise enjoyable evening into a tension filled experience. Talking with your partner about your feelings in advance can help.

3. Understand the difference between privacy and secrecy

Your child needs to understand their story, from as early an age as possible, but you do not owe the world a detailed account of your journey. Secrecy implies shame, and this is not about shame; it is about protecting your feelings while you heal and giving yourself the room to decide with your partner how private you would like to be about your family building process. You may decide that you would like to share information with others as the child grows, or you may decide to share every detail with friends and family. The choice is yours and your partner's together. Talking to your partner will give you a chance to decide what you would like to share with others and prepare you for those awkward moments that will inevitably arise.

4. Create rituals

Rituals can be one of the best tools for building a family identity. Pizza on Friday nights, Sunday afternoon walks, or a bedtime that is special to your family are all habits and traditions you can create together. These experiences can help you bond and build your unique family characteristics. The traditions and life you build together are not about genetics; they are about the family you have created.

5. Get support

Having a therapist who understands third party reproduction can make an enormous difference. The feelings that come with being a non-genetically related parent are real and complex, and they deserve real attention. Working through them with someone who understands this landscape can help you separate what belongs to you from what belongs to your child, and move forward with more clarity and confidence.

It is also worth acknowledging that the genetically linked parent has their own set of feelings to navigate. They may feel guilty about what their partner is going through. They may feel uncertain about how to support someone whose experience they cannot fully share. They may worry about the balance of the relationship and whether the non-genetically related parent feels equally valued as a parent.

Recognizing each other's emotional needs and making space for both experiences is what makes the difference. Neither parent's feelings are more valid than the other's. Both matter and both deserve attention.

The parents I have seen thrive are the ones who named their fears, talked to their partners, and got support when they needed it. Parenting is never perfect, but honesty, care, and effort can make all the difference for the individual, the couple, and the family.
